unit.title: Build variants, libraries, and tooling
unit.summary: Seven source-backed deep dives connect build identities, dependency contracts, the active library landscape, generated resources, debugging, CI matrices, and bounded rollout decisions.

lessons.title: Targets, schemes, configurations, and environment identity
lessons.summary: Trace a build choice through xcconfig inheritance, compiler conditions, app identity, entitlements, and Gradle variant boundaries.
objectives: Separate target membership, scheme actions, configuration settings, destination, and runtime environment.
Explain xcconfig includes, inheritance, conditional settings, and effective-value inspection.
Audit bundle identity, compiler flags, and signing boundaries without exposing sensitive values.
Compare the current Tuist and Gradle graphs without inventing an automatic flavor cross-product.

sections.title: Begin with the artifact you intend to install
sections.html:
Imagine an Android change that works in prodNormalDebug but fails in a release build. You would inspect the module, selected variant, source sets, generated constants, shrinker settings, and signing inputs. Apply that habit to iOS, while replacing the assumption that one variant name describes everything. An iOS build request combines a workspace or project, a scheme action, one or more targets, a configuration, and a destination. The service environment is another decision. Write those choices before debugging the behavior.

A target defines a component and its output: an app, extension, framework, or test bundle. A scheme chooses which components participate in actions such as Run, Test, and Archive. A configuration supplies settings for those components. A destination selects a platform and runtime. A production endpoint can be used by a Debug app, and a Release build can be configured for a test environment. Optimization and environment are separate axes even when a team intentionally couples them.

The active app manifest declares Zocdoc as an app target, alongside an App Clip and extensions. Its explicit Zocdoc scheme runs Debug. The retained legacy scheme is named Zocdoc Prod. Neither name proves that every action uses identical settings. Session 005 introduced the vocabulary; today your job is to trace each choice until it reaches the compiled artifact. A correct trace names the consuming target rather than treating the entire workspace as one uniform configuration.

sections.title: A scheme is not a product flavor
sections.html:
The inspected Android app build declares app and environment flavor dimensions. The app dimension contains prod and zdtest; the environment dimension contains normal and integrationTest. Debug and release are build types, and beforeVariants disables zdtest release combinations. This is concrete support for reasoning about prodNormalDebug. Repository prose also mentions browserstack, but that flavor does not appear in the inspected productFlavors block. Prefer the current declaration when describing what this checkout generates.

Xcode does not automatically multiply every configuration, target, and scheme into the equivalent Gradle variant graph. A team may create several app targets with different identities, use one target with configurations, or use a scheme pre-action to select generated inputs. You must discover the strategy. The active Tuist app target declares Debug and Release configurations, both using Zocdoc.xcconfig. Nearby Local and Sandbox files describe additional inputs; their existence alone does not prove a generated QA scheme selects them.

Gradle source-set overlays also lack a universal Xcode counterpart. The Tuist source glob and exclusions determine membership, while compiler conditions may select declarations within those files. SwiftPM has its own target paths and settings. A source file in a directory called Debug is not automatically debug-only. To compare the platforms, record intent, membership, dependencies, constants, resources, and installation identity in separate columns. This catches the common mistake of copying a flavor name into a scheme and assuming all its former behavior followed.

sections.title: Read configuration files as layered inputs
sections.html:
An xcconfig file contains build-setting assignments, comments, and includes. It is neither Swift nor a shell script. The active Zocdoc.xcconfig includes ZocdocBaseApp and ZocdocShared. The base file includes the Appstore input, sets a production compilation flag, and leaves the E2E condition empty. The shared file constructs the main bundle identifier using a prefix variable. Sandbox supplies a different prefix; Local includes Sandbox and overrides the environment. Follow the include chain in order instead of reading one isolated line.

#include "Base.xcconfig"
// Synthetic scratch configuration
COURSE_ENVIRONMENT = Sandbox
SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS = $(inherited) COURSE_SANDBOX
OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS = $(inherited)
ONLY_ACTIVE_ARCH[sdk=iphonesimulator*] = YES

The first line includes another configuration file relative to this file. Double slash begins a comment. The environment assignment creates a user-defined setting; application code cannot read it automatically. The next assignment preserves an inherited condition list and adds a Swift identifier. Parenthesized dollar syntax expands build settings, rather than executing shell substitution. The bracket expression restricts the final assignment to matching SDK names. It does not select a simulator destination by itself.

Repeated assignments and higher-precedence project or target settings can replace values. Preserve inherited lists deliberately; appending without inheritance can lose search paths or flags. Equally, inheritance can retain an unwanted old value, so inspect the final setting. Be careful with literal URL text: double slash has comment meaning in this format. Use the repository's established representation and verify expansion rather than pasting a secret-bearing URL into a configuration example.

sections.title: Resolve the value used by the chosen action
sections.html:
Reading an xcconfig proves declared intent, not the final compiler invocation. Xcode combines defaults, configuration files, project settings, target settings, conditions, and command-line overrides. Inspect the Levels view or build-settings output for the specific target, configuration, and SDK. In this checkout the production helper explicitly avoids setting version keys because doing so would override the version workflow. That comment explains a concrete ownership boundary: moving an assignment into a convenient dictionary can change precedence.

The main app's Debug settings supply its compilation conditions and disable optimization. Release supplies its production condition plus the optional E2E condition. Some of these assignments do not contain inherited expansion. Therefore a scratch xcconfig append cannot be assumed to survive the app target's explicit override. Review the effective condition list and the compile command. A build-setting variable whose name starts with ZD is a team convention, not a language feature.

For read-only discovery in an already prepared client checkout, list the existing workspace and schemes, then inspect settings for the chosen action. Filter output to bundle identifier, module name, deployment target, optimization, and compilation conditions. Full settings dumps may expose injected configuration or signing metadata and are inappropriate course evidence. A command that resolves packages or runs scheme actions has a different scope from reading a manifest. Record whether your result is a declared value, an effective value, or a compiled behavior; those are three different levels of proof.

sections.title: Compile-time conditions do not configure a server
sections.html:
Swift conditional compilation uses identifiers, not C preprocessor values. A Swift active condition is written COURSE_SANDBOX, without the C-style assignment COURSE_SANDBOX=1. Objective-C's GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS belongs to a separate compiler. The app manifest configures both families. Updating one does not automatically update the other. Runtime feature flags are yet another mechanism: they choose behavior in an existing binary rather than removing code from it.

enum CourseEnvironment: String {
    case production, sandbox
}

#if COURSE_SANDBOX
let compiledEnvironment: CourseEnvironment = .sandbox
#else
let compiledEnvironment: CourseEnvironment = .production
#endif

func environmentLabel(for environment: CourseEnvironment) -> String {
    environment.rawValue
}
print(environmentLabel(for: compiledEnvironment))

This standalone Swift example has no network or UIKit dependency. The enum's raw type gives each case a string representation; the annotation on compiledEnvironment makes the intended type explicit. The compiler retains one branch according to its conditions. The for label is used at the call, while environment names the local parameter. With no COURSE_SANDBOX condition, the predicted output is production. A synthetic build adding that condition predicts sandbox. These predictions are not evidence of the client's endpoint configuration.

Changing a compiler condition does not automatically change an Info.plist, registration callback URL, asset, entitlement, or remote SDK configuration. The retained client uses pre-build tooling, so inspect that path before describing environment switching. The E2E Release condition is a useful example: the default file leaves it empty, and a test build can opt in. Prove the intended branch is absent from an ordinary distribution artifact rather than assuming the word Release guarantees it.

sections.title: Installation identity and capability form a contract
sections.html:
PRODUCT_MODULE_NAME controls a source module identity; PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER controls an installed bundle identity. They solve different problems. A QA prefix can allow a second app to coexist, but sharing or separating data depends on app groups, Keychain access groups, server accounts, and container policy. An endpoint change alone does not isolate those resources. Compare the complete environment contract before installing two variants with similarly named icons.

The active main app resolves its bundle identifier from a user-defined setting and selects its Info.plist and entitlement file through settings. The App Clip derives a related identity, while other extensions declare their own identities. That is evidence of separate products, not an instruction to copy the app's capabilities into every extension. For example, the medication widget deliberately depends only on a core module because a broader UI dependency reaches an application API unavailable to extensions.

Signing adds authorization to this graph. The requested bundle IDs and capabilities must align with provisioning and the signing workflow. You can explain the roles of a certificate, matching private key, profile, and entitlements without copying any value from them. Treat a signing diagnostic as a particular mismatch to investigate, not a reason to rotate shared identities. Simulator success still leaves device installation and distribution verification pending. Session 026 explains the delivery chain; here your acceptance note should identify which target requests each capability and which environment changes could invalidate that request.

sections.title: Turn variant failures into bounded hypotheses
sections.html:
Suppose Debug imports a module but Release does not. Check whether an import is conditionally compiled, whether the dependency is declared for the consuming target, whether optimization reveals a different linker path, and whether the generated graph matches the retained package route. Do not conclude that the library is debug-only from the symptom. Conversely, a file that compiles on both routes can still load the wrong resource or service configuration at runtime.

Suppose QA installs over production. Compare the resolved bundle identifiers of the built apps. A different display name cannot establish separate installation identity. Suppose an extension fails validation while the app installs. Inspect that extension's identity, version metadata, capability requests, and linkage rather than changing the app's settings indiscriminately. The unit's later sessions will add resources, dependencies, and CI destinations to this same investigative method.

Build a small evidence ledger for each case: expected behavior, selected graph route, declared setting, effective setting if inspected, and observed artifact result if tested. Mark missing evidence as pending. Keep representative Debug and Release checks, and include the App Clip or extension when the change reaches their shared dependencies. A configuration matrix should be large enough to expose the affected boundary, yet bounded enough to finish. The exercise below practices this reasoning without rewriting the client's setup, generating credentials, or treating a paper trace as a successful archive.

quiz.question: Why can an xcconfig condition fail to reach the Swift compiler?
options: The target can replace the condition list at a higher-precedence layer.
Swift automatically ignores every custom identifier.
A scheme name always overrides compiler settings.
Conditions only work in the simulator.
quiz.explanation: The final target settings can replace rather than append the xcconfig value. Inspect the effective list and compiler invocation. Conditions are valid custom identifiers and are not determined by a scheme's spelling.

quiz.question: Which observation supports the current Android variant graph?
options: Every flavor mentioned in a README must be generated.
The inspected build declares app/environment dimensions and filters zdtest release.
Xcode automatically generates the same Cartesian product.
A QA display name proves a separate application ID.
quiz.explanation: Declarations and beforeVariants determine the observed graph. Documentation names need confirmation; Xcode schemes do not supply Gradle flavor multiplication, and display names do not settle installation identity.

quiz.question: A Release binary connects to a sandbox service. What follows?
options: Release compilation is impossible.
The binary must have a different module name.
Optimization configuration and runtime environment are independent choices.
Its signing identity must be revoked.
quiz.explanation: Release describes a build-setting choice, not a universal endpoint guarantee. Trace environment injection, identity, and capabilities separately before diagnosing signing or changing module names.

exercise.brief: Create a configuration contract and failure investigation for a synthetic Sandbox app, using the active manifests as read-only evidence.
steps: Trace the main app target, Debug/Release configuration files, explicit scheme, and xcconfig include chain.
Write a table comparing optimization, Swift/C conditions, bundle identity, resources, runtime environment, and capabilities for two synthetic builds.
Predict both branches of the standalone Swift snippet, then optionally run it in your scratch environment with and without the condition.
Explain why merely appending a condition in an xcconfig might not change the client target.
Choose next checks for a QA app overwriting production and a Release-only missing import.
acceptance: The contract separates target, scheme action, configuration, destination, and environment.
The Android comparison cites the two declared dimensions and the disabled zdtest release combination.
The include trace identifies declared values and explicitly leaves uninspected effective values pending.
Predicted snippet outputs are production and sandbox, with verification scope stated.
Identity and capability checks contain no credential, profile, certificate, or private-key values.
exercise.solution:
A worked trace starts at Zocdoc's app target, follows its two configurations into Zocdoc.xcconfig, then follows BaseApp into the Appstore file and Shared into the bundle-identifier construction. The explicit Tuist Zocdoc scheme uses Debug for Run; the retained legacy scheme is a separate input. Local and Sandbox are available configuration files, but their selection by a generated scheme has not been established by their mere existence.

Synthetic choiceProduction DebugSandbox Release
OptimizationDebug settingRelease setting
Compiler conditionNo COURSE_SANDBOXCOURSE_SANDBOX added effectively
Installation identityexample.course.appexample.course.app.sandbox
Environment/resources/capabilitiesExplicit production contractSeparately reviewed sandbox contract

The enum example predicts production without the custom condition and sandbox when it is passed to the compiler. The client target can override an xcconfig condition list, so this scratch result does not prove the client's flags. For an overwrite, inspect the built bundle identifier; for a missing import, inspect consuming-target dependencies, conditional imports, and generated versus retained graphs. Effective-setting and built-artifact checks remain pending until actually performed. A completed learner submission contains its own predictions and evidence rather than copying the worked table as proof.

lessons.title: SwiftPM products, pins, binary frameworks, and compatibility
lessons.summary: Evaluate a dependency as a build, runtime, compatibility, and supply-chain contract rather than a package name and version.
objectives: Trace package identity, product exposure, target modules, requirements, and resolved revisions.
Explain automatic, static, and dynamic linkage separately from framework packaging.
Distinguish source compatibility, ABI stability, module stability, and library evolution.
Review platform availability, resources, licenses, provenance, and rollback inputs before adopting a library.

sections.title: A dependency has several identities and consumers
sections.html:
In Gradle, a dependency coordinate does not tell you every class, transitive artifact, native library, or resource it contributes. SwiftPM deserves the same scrutiny. A package has an identity and a manifest. Its products are the public build outputs consumers request. Its targets define modules and tests. A library product may expose several targets. Import statements name modules, so package, product, target, and import names need not match.

The checkout supplies an instructive example. ZDAssets exposes a ZDAssets product containing several asset and font targets. ZDCore exposes a product containing core Swift, Objective-C, Sentry-related, and tracing targets, alongside a separate ZDPromiseCore product. ZDNetworking exposes Base, Lite, Full, definitions, and testing products. Selecting an umbrella product can therefore pull a larger graph than a particular feature requires. Names such as Lite suggest intent; inspect the dependencies to establish the actual boundary.

Write a dependency contract before choosing a new library: which consumer needs which operation, which product supplies it, what modules it imports, and what other targets it brings. Then list resource, platform, startup, privacy, and test implications. A manifest establishes declared edges, while the linked artifact establishes inclusion. An import discovered in an inactive copy proves neither. This session builds on session 043's target map and prepares you to audit real library roles in session 045.

sections.title: Read the manifest one initializer at a time
sections.html:
This complete synthetic client manifest assumes you separately created a sibling CourseCodec package exposing a CourseCodec library. It demonstrates dependency syntax; it is not a runnable client until that package and both source directories exist. It uses tools 5.9 and an iOS 17 platform floor, keeping manifest APIs separate from the installed compiler and effective language mode.

// swift-tools-version: 5.9
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "CourseConsumer",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "CourseConsumer", targets: ["CourseConsumer"])
    ],
    dependencies: [
        .package(path: "../CourseCodec")
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "CourseConsumer",
            dependencies: [
                .product(name: "CourseCodec", package: "CourseCodec")
            ]
        ),
        .testTarget(
            name: "CourseConsumerTests",
            dependencies: ["CourseConsumer"]
        )
    ]
)

PackageDescription is the manifest API, not a runtime library for the application. The package name labels the container. Platforms declares a deployment constraint; it does not make UIKit run on a default macOS host. Products exposes the production target. Dependencies makes a local package available for resolution, using a path relative to the manifest. The production target then selects a product from that package. Declaring the package alone would not grant every target access to it.

The test target depends on the production target, and its import still names the compiled module. Square brackets construct arrays; the leading dot on library, target, and product uses type inference to select a static member. Argument labels distinguish name, package, and targets. Read nested arrays from the outside inward. This small discipline prevents a common review mistake: moving a dependency into a package-level list while forgetting the particular consuming target.

sections.title: Separate a requirement from its selected revision
sections.html:
A version requirement describes allowed choices. An exact requirement selects a specific semantic version; from permits compatible versions up to the next major version for an ordinary stable release. Branch and revision requirements have different update semantics. A branch called 4.1.3 remains a branch requirement, even if its name looks like a release. The checkout uses precisely that form for lottie-spm and uses main for the internal AWS wrapper.

Package.resolved records the selected state of a resolution graph, including revisions and versions or branches. It is not a list of libraries proven to execute in production. A package can be present transitively or only for tests. A top-level consumer's resolution file governs its resolution context; a dependency's own lockfile does not universally force downstream consumers to use its selections. Locate the leaf application or tooling graph before promising reproducibility.

The two inspected resolution files are not identical. For example, Tuist resolves swift-crypto at 4.5.0 while the retained workspace file records 4.2.0. Other transitive selections differ too. Do not repair this learning exercise by forcing every pin to match. First determine the consuming routes, constraints, reasons for the difference, and expected parity. Reproducible review records the manifest, relevant lockfile, selected revision, toolchain, and generator. A broad update can silently change unrelated transitive code, so a bounded upgrade includes a diff of every changed pin rather than just the requested direct dependency.

sections.title: Static versus dynamic describes linking, not the filename
sections.html:
Static linking incorporates selected library object code into a consumer's linked binary. Dynamic linking leaves a dependency to be loaded at runtime, with corresponding embedding, signing, and search-path responsibilities for non-system frameworks. A framework is a packaging form; it can contain a static or a dynamic binary. An XCFramework is a container for platform and architecture variants, not a third linkage mode. An AAR analogy helps you ask about packaged code and resources, but it does not predict the Mach-O linkage model.

SwiftPM library products can request static or dynamic behavior, or omit the type so the consuming build chooses an appropriate form. The retained ZDModulesMocks product explicitly requests dynamic linkage. Its Tuist target is declared as a static framework. That is an observed route difference to review, not proof of a runtime defect or of semantic equivalence. The core Tuist manifests also declare many static frameworks while selecting the external Sentry-Dynamic product.

Linkage choices have tradeoffs. Static code may be repeated across separately linked executables, such as an app and an extension, but dead stripping can remove unused portions. Dynamic frameworks bring loader and packaging costs and can still introduce substantial size. Duplicate symbols can arise from multiple copies of the same definitions; missing framework embedding can cause launch failure after compilation succeeds. Measure size and launch effects for representative artifacts before claiming a faster choice. Session 044 teaches the mechanism; actual linker maps and device profiling remain further verification.

sections.title: ABI stability and module stability answer different questions
sections.html:
Source compatibility asks whether client source still compiles against an API. An application binary interface, or ABI, describes compiled calling and layout conventions. Swift's stable runtime ABI on supported Apple platforms does not make every third-party library binary interchangeable. The library's own public contract, build options, and evolution promises still matter. A source package rebuilt with the app has a different distribution problem from a binary supplied by a vendor.

Module stability concerns whether a compiler can consume a module interface produced by another compiler version. Serialized swiftmodule files are compiler-specific; textual swiftinterface files support a more stable distribution boundary. Library evolution gives independently distributed libraries room to make compatible changes without requiring old clients to be rebuilt. Xcode's BUILD_LIBRARY_FOR_DISTRIBUTION enables the relevant distribution support. It is not a universal optimization to enable on every internal target compiled and shipped together.

An XCFramework combines appropriate slices for platforms and variants. An arm64 iPhone binary is not interchangeable with an arm64 simulator binary just because the CPU architecture label matches. Inspect platform metadata, minimum OS, interfaces, and supported destinations. A binary module still cannot expose an unsupported API to every deployment runtime. Frozen layout or exhaustive enum assumptions can constrain future evolution; changing public declarations needs a compatibility review. Treat a compiler-version import failure, a linker symbol failure, and a runtime unavailable-API failure as separate boundaries with different evidence.

sections.title: A successful import is only one compatibility gate
sections.html:
Use availability as a two-part question: can this target compile the declaration using its selected SDK, and can the oldest supported runtime execute the path? A newer installed SDK answers the first question, not the second. A declaration's @available annotation expresses its supported platform range; a runtime #available check narrows where a call executes. Conditional canImport checks module availability to the compiler. It does not replace an operating-system runtime check.

Resources are another independent gate. A linked static library can still require a generated module resource bundle. Binary frameworks can include assets or privacy information that must survive packaging. A test that constructs a pure model will not detect a missing font, storyboard, localization, or privacy manifest. Add a resource lookup and inspect the relevant packaged product when adopting a resource-bearing dependency. Session 046 will practice this with Bundle.module and synthetic JSON.

Transitive platforms can also raise the effective floor. A package's broad platform declaration does not guarantee every target can build on every advertised platform, especially when sources import UIKit or rely on extension-unavailable APIs. Follow imports and dependencies for the actual product you select. The checkout's generated GraphQL packages advertise platforms below the main app's iOS 17 floor; that does not lower the app floor. Record SDK, deployment, language mode, host-tool requirements, and resource needs as separate compatibility fields rather than compressing them into one version number.

sections.title: Review provenance, licenses, and update ownership
sections.html:
A checksum verifies that a downloaded binary archive matches the declared bytes. It does not prove those bytes are trustworthy, appropriately licensed, vulnerability-free, or free of data collection. A verified XCFramework signature adds origin evidence; it still does not substitute for understanding behavior. Record repository origin, resolved revision, binary source where applicable, checksum, signature evidence, and which trusted workflow produced or obtained the artifact. Build plugins and macros deserve review because they participate in the build, even when their code is not bundled into the app.

License review starts with the actual selected version and its included license and notice files. Transitive libraries and bundled fonts or media can carry separate terms. A familiar package name is not evidence of a particular license, so this course does not assign license verdicts without reading those artifacts. Legal interpretation and vulnerability triage require the appropriate specialists. Your engineering contribution is a complete inventory, usage boundary, distribution form, and reproducible evidence.

Ownership makes the review operational. Identify a maintainer for upgrades, a consumer for behavior validation, and a recovery owner for a failed rollout. Prefer a wrapper or protocol when it isolates a real substitution seam; avoid wrapping an entire vendor API mechanically. Keep credential material in the approved configuration path and out of dependency reports. The bounded decision should explain benefit, compatibility costs, affected app and extension products, test evidence, remaining license or security review, and how to reconstruct the previous graph. None of these checks establishes that the checkout's old pins are safe or unsafe merely from their age.

quiz.question: The manifest says branch: 4.1.3 for lottie-spm. How should it be classified?
options: An exact semantic version because it contains digits.
A branch requirement whose resolved commit belongs in the evidence ledger.
An ABI guarantee.
An automatic static library.
quiz.explanation: The API label determines requirement semantics. A version-shaped branch name remains mutable as a branch; the resolution file records the selected revision. Neither linkage nor ABI follows from its spelling.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly separates packaging and linking?
options: Every framework is dynamic.
An XCFramework is a fourth compiler language mode.
A framework may contain static or dynamic code; an XCFramework groups platform variants.
Static libraries never need resources.
quiz.explanation: Packaging, linkage, and resources are separate dimensions. The consumer must inspect the contained binary and bundle requirements rather than infer dynamic behavior from a suffix.

quiz.question: What does a matching binary checksum establish?
options: The archive bytes match the declared checksum.
The dependency has no exploitable defect.
The license permits every distribution.
All simulator and device slices are interchangeable.
quiz.explanation: A checksum is integrity evidence for bytes. Provenance, security, license interpretation, platform metadata, and runtime behavior need their own reviews and verification.

exercise.brief: Write a dependency contract for the observed ZDModulesMocks linkage difference and one synthetic vendor binary without changing client manifests.
steps: Trace the retained ZDModulesMocks product and sibling Tuist target, recording declared linkage separately for each route.
Compare one direct requirement and its resolved state; include lottie-spm's branch semantics.
For a synthetic VendorCodec XCFramework, list required simulator/device slices, interfaces, runtime floor, resource packaging, origin, and license evidence.
Classify a compiler module-version error, duplicate symbol, missing framework at launch, and absent resource.
Propose the smallest verification and a reconstruction plan for the prior graph.
acceptance: Package, product, module, target, and selected revision are distinguished.
The dynamic-versus-static route difference is reported as an observation requiring review, not a confirmed bug.
Device arm64 and simulator arm64 are treated as distinct platform variants.
Checksum, signature, license, security, and runtime checks have separate evidence fields.
No pin is described as latest and no upgrade, license approval, or app build is claimed performed.
exercise.solution:
The retained package exposes ZDModulesMocks with type dynamic; the sibling Project.swift declares it as a staticFramework. A sound report preserves both observations and identifies test consumers before recommending parity. It does not assume the same suffix or name produces identical packaging. For lottie-spm, record branch 4.1.3 and the resolution file's commit, not an invented exact-version requirement.

VendorCodec's contract names its consumer product, supported device and simulator variants, minimum OS, public interfaces, linked dependencies, resource bundles, privacy information, checksum, and origin evidence. License and vulnerability decisions remain pending until the selected artifact and its dependencies are reviewed. Module-version failure suggests interface/toolchain inspection; duplicate symbols suggest repeated definitions or linkage; a loader failure suggests embedding and run paths; a nil resource URL suggests bundle membership and lookup.

Reconstruction uses the prior manifest, relevant resolution file, source revision or binary checksum, generator and compiler versions, and unchanged resource inputs. A narrow source-package build can establish a compilation boundary, while an app or test-host build checks integration. Packaging and device execution require their own evidence. This is a worked review, not proof that either observed linkage route or the synthetic binary has been executed.

lessons.title: The active library and internal-module landscape
lessons.summary: Build a verified responsibility map, distinguish retained and preferred patterns, and assign concrete review ownership to library changes.
objectives: Inventory declared libraries using active manifests, pins, and consumer sources.
Explain the boundaries between transport, models, state, UI, identity, engagement, and observability.
Identify ReactiveKit, PromiseKit, Combine, and Observation without claiming a completed migration.
Design a small vendor-independent contract and state the ownership and verification limits of a migration.

sections.title: Verify the graph before explaining the names
sections.html:
An Android dependency report is useful, but it cannot tell you whether an SDK owns transport, lifecycle, storage, or the business rule you are changing. Build the iOS landscape around responsibilities and evidence. Start with the active Tuist dependency manifest, then the consumer Project.swift, the retained Package.swift where relevant, and the resolution file for the route you are evaluating. Source imports confirm which module a file uses; target membership confirms whether that file belongs to the graph.

The course's searchable dependency catalogue supplies the reproducible remote pin snapshot. Use it to compare direct requirements, selected revisions, and graph differences; this lesson adds consumer behavior and ownership. A resolved entry can be transitive, test-only, or tooling-related. The catalogue's remote scope does not enumerate every local module, vendored source, system framework, or resource that reaches an artifact.

The inspected Tuist graph and retained workspace graph also differ in membership: Peasy and SwiftLintPlugins appear in the retained resolution file but not the Tuist resolution file. The retained Xcode project contains their package references, including a Peasy product reference. This is route evidence, not proof that both execute at runtime or that a plugin is bundled. Classify a lint plugin as build tooling before treating it like a feature SDK. Explain a difference before proposing removal or parity.

For each row, ask which target consumes the product and what it initializes. A declared app dependency establishes a build edge; it does not prove consent behavior, startup order, or current operational ownership. Record those as additional questions, with source evidence where inspected.

sections.title: Remote, local, vendored, and system are distinct origins
sections.html:
A remote dependency is resolved from a repository or artifact location. Tuist/Package.swift declares such requirements, including internally maintained remote packages. Remote therefore does not mean external company ownership. A local package or Tuist project is built from the checkout; ZDCore, ZDNetworking, ZDAssets, and feature projects are examples. Their code is pinned by the source revision and their manifests, rather than by a remote Package.resolved entry for each local target.

Vendored code is maintained inside the repository under a chosen update policy. TestableMacro is a verified example under Vendors, with both a package and a Tuist project. Its SwiftSyntax dependency remains remote and its macro implementation runs as a host build tool. A vendor-looking framework search path is merely a setting until its actual artifact is found and consumed. System frameworks, such as UIKit, Foundation, CoreData, and CoreLocation, come through the selected SDK and OS runtime; imports and link settings provide their evidence, rather than SwiftPM pins.

These origins change review work. A remote upgrade needs origin and transitive-diff review; a local module change needs consumer and composition-root checks; a vendored update needs upstream provenance plus local patch accounting; a system API adoption needs deployment and runtime availability checks. None of them automatically settles human ownership, licensing, or resource packaging. Keep the graph maintainer, behavior owner, and specialist reviewer distinct.

Lifetime is a second axis. A UI helper may live with a view, a media room with a call, a request adapter with an operation, and a telemetry or engagement service with an account or process. Confirm actual allocation, registration scope, callbacks, and teardown. Moving a scene-owned SDK into a process singleton can retain data or work across account changes even when the package pin stays identical. Conversely, constructing a new process-level service for every view can duplicate observers or exporters. Ask who starts, cancels, resets, and releases each integration.

sections.title: Transport, generated models, and domain operations differ
sections.html:
ZDNetworking is not synonymous with Alamofire. Its manifest defines internal operation, client, definitions, multipart, dispatcher-tool, and adapter targets. AlamofireExtension depends on Alamofire and PromiseKit alongside internal contracts. Another adapter, ZDUrlSessionExtension, also retains PromiseKit. Replacing a third-party HTTP layer therefore involves request construction, error mapping, security behavior, cancellation, and consumers of those internal interfaces, not just changing an import.

The GraphQL side is equally specific. ZDGqlPhi and ZDGqlNonPhi are generated schema modules that depend on ApolloAPI. Their generated model requirement does not establish that every consumer needs the full Apollo client, transport, or cache. The main app declares ApolloAPI explicitly, while the app unit-test target includes Apollo. Read product edges at that level of precision. The PHI and NonPhi namespaces describe separate schema-generation boundaries; the names do not certify that arbitrary logged payloads are safe.

ZDData owns model-related targets and ZDApiOperations owns operation definitions in the repository architecture. Those responsibilities can overlap in a concrete feature, so trace one request end to end before changing the seam. An Android analogy is distinguishing Retrofit or Apollo runtime, generated wire types, DTO-to-domain mapping, and a repository/interactor. The boundary breaks when you assume a named product is equivalent to a Kotlin package or that all GraphQL models imply one global cache. Verify the exact consumer and runtime owner.

sections.title: Security-sensitive SDKs need lifecycle and data owners
sections.html:
ZDAuthentication declares Auth0.swift and its internal feature dependencies. The main app separately declares the internal AWS framework wrapper on a branch. Both can coexist in a transitional identity landscape. A manifest cannot establish which login flow uses which system, which token store is authoritative, or whether an old integration is fully retired. Trace registration and call sites with synthetic account cases before proposing removal. Never copy credentials, tokens, signing inputs, or whole account stores into an inventory.

The active app graph includes BrazeKit, BrazeUI, BranchSDK, and DataDome products. The notification service extension depends on BrazeNotificationService. This connects a dependency update to multiple products and lifecycle paths. Engagement, attribution, protection, and authentication are distinct responsibilities even if several SDKs initialize near launch. Identify what each integration receives, when it can run, how account changes reset state, and how opt-in or authorization policy is enforced where required.

On Android you would review Application startup, consent gates, manifest components, and SDK network behavior. On iOS add scene and extension boundaries, signed capabilities, resource packaging, and the actual distribution artifact. A disabled feature flag may prevent one screen while leaving an SDK initializer active. Therefore a rollout owner needs an explicit containment seam. This lesson teaches the review questions; it does not conclude that the checkout has a particular consent defect or that any library is currently vulnerable.

sections.title: UI helpers and specialized runtimes have different costs
sections.html:
SnapKit supplies a constraint-construction API used by inspected UIKit source files. It does not replace Auto Layout's measurement, priorities, safe areas, or constraint solver. Lottie supplies the app's animation product, with imports in loading and intake UI. It does not remove the need to budget decoding, animation work, accessibility, or reduced-motion behavior. A familiar Android analogy is a layout DSL or animation library; the underlying rendering and lifecycle rules still belong to the platform.

ZDUI is itself a package with several products and targets, including Mezzanine components, legacy UI, Objective-C support, and App Clip UI. Its manifest pulls assets, internal data and networking contracts, and retained asynchronous libraries. The App Clip comment warns about dependency and resource size. Do not treat the design system as free of runtime implications simply because it looks like presentation code. Also avoid deriving an App Clip policy limit from a historical comment; current distribution requirements need current official verification.

TwilioVideo is consumed by ZDVideoVisit's target and imported in room and media sources. Its update surface includes device permissions, interruption, audio routing, participant state, network reconnection, and teardown. Those cases need specialist device practice beyond a compiler check. Figma's code-connect package and the font-subset tooling serve different purposes again: design description and build/resource preparation. Put these dependencies in their own responsibility rows rather than categorizing every library near a view as a interchangeable UI utility.

sections.title: Names and preference documents do not prove migration
sections.html:
The repository guide calls ZDRxCore a legacy RxSwift-based module, but the inspected active manifest depends on ReactiveKit 3.17.1 and the module source re-exports ReactiveKit. That is the concrete evidence for this course. Do not teach RxSwift operators as if they are the verified implementation solely because Rx appears in the local name. An underscored exported-import attribute is observed source behavior; it is not a recommendation to introduce the same nonstandard API into your own package.

PromiseKit remains explicitly declared and imported. The guide says it is deprecated in favor of Swift Concurrency, which establishes direction rather than completion. The inspected bridge offers Promise initializers backed by Task and async methods backed by continuations. Bridging a promise to async does not automatically propagate task cancellation into the underlying work, or make its lifetime structured. Read ownership, completion, and actor isolation separately.

The guide prefers Observation and mentions Combine helpers. Active Combine-to-stream extensions are verified in ZDCoreBase; do not advertise a standalone ZDCombineCore product from the guide alone. One extension finishes an AsyncStream for both successful and failed publisher completion, so it does not preserve the publisher's error as a thrown stream failure. A migration test must protect product error distinctions, termination, cancellation, and buffering semantics. Session 017 gives stream foundations; here the key lesson is to compare contracts before celebrating replacement of a framework name.

sections.title: Separate interfaces from container implementation
sections.html:
ZDModules describes interfaces for dependency injection and flow entry points. Its README asks callers to pass runtime data and configuration rather than app-specific services or giant singleton objects. ZDCoreBase declares Swinject, while the app graph consumes internal modules and the container-related infrastructure. Swinject is therefore an implementation ingredient, not the whole architectural contract. A feature depending on an interface does not need to understand every registration detail.

The Android comparison is separating an interface from the Dagger binding that supplies its implementation. The analogy has limits: the inspected Swift container can resolve values at runtime, so missing or ambiguous registration may emerge during execution rather than as the same compile-time graph validation you expect from generated Dagger code. Validate registration at the actual composition root and exercise the selected flow. Importing ZDModules is not proof that every dependency can be resolved.

Internal ownership should follow responsibility: the interface owner maintains the contract, the implementation owner maintains the adapter, and the composition-root owner maintains registration and lifecycle. These are review roles, not a claim about named teams or people. The manifests and README do not prove current human ownership. Tests may use the ZDModulesMocks product, whose route-specific linkage was covered in session 044. A change to an interface, mock, and registration can reach many consumers even if the vendor dependency itself stays pinned.

sections.title: Design a seam that preserves meaningful failures
sections.html:
Use a wrapper when it expresses a stable product operation and isolates a dependency you may replace. This synthetic library source uses ordinary Swift and can belong to a host-compatible package. It neither calls a vendor SDK nor implements a production client.

enum CatalogFailure: Error { case offline }
struct CatalogEntry: Equatable {
    let id: String
    let title: String
}
protocol CatalogServing {
    func entries() async throws -> [CatalogEntry]
}
struct CatalogFixture: CatalogServing {
    let result: Result<[CatalogEntry], CatalogFailure>
    func entries() async throws -> [CatalogEntry] {
        try result.get()
    }
}

CatalogFailure conforms to Error so a failure can participate in throwing APIs. CatalogEntry stores immutable fields and gains synthesized equality. The protocol declares the operation's suspension and error effects explicitly. The fake stores a Result; get returns its success or throws its failure. An empty successful array remains different from an offline error. A consumer must use try await; making an operation async does not guarantee background execution or automatic cancellation of a vendor request.

A real adapter would translate vendor results into this contract and define cancellation, ordering, and retry behavior. Avoid exposing a vendor-specific type unless the consumer truly needs it. Equally, avoid a generic wrapper with dozens of methods that merely renames the SDK: that creates maintenance work without a substitution seam. Kotlin suspend and a sealed error model are useful starting analogies, but Swift's throws, actor isolation, and task cancellation have their own rules. Session 049 will use a smaller pure policy change to practice bounded adoption evidence.

sections.title: A migration claim needs a measurable boundary
sections.html:
Write the migration claim as a behavior: this consumer obtains equivalent synthetic entries through the new adapter, preserves empty success and offline failure, and releases underlying work on cancellation according to the agreed policy. List consumers still using the old route. If legacy promises remain elsewhere, say the selected seam changed rather than claiming PromiseKit is gone. A smaller, truthful completion statement makes a later rollback possible.

Assign the graph maintainer to manifests and pins, the feature maintainer to behavior, the platform maintainer to destination and packaging coverage, and relevant specialists to security or licensing questions. Actual people must be confirmed through established ownership evidence; the course does not infer them from authorship comments. Include test baselines, generated code, privacy resources, and the App Clip or extension when their dependencies are affected. A dependency update can be operationally significant without changing visible UI.

The evidence ledger should separate declared, compiled, tested, packaged, and distributed observations. Reading active source supports the first category and sometimes a code-level behavior explanation, but it is not a profiling session or SDK network audit. The exercise asks you to construct this ledger and identify remaining work. No learner progress is automatically completed by the table, and no migration status should be upgraded simply because the course describes a preferred future API.

quiz.question: What is verified about ZDRxCore in this checkout?
options: Its name proves it uses RxSwift.
Its manifest and exported import identify ReactiveKit.
It has already been entirely replaced by Observation.
It only contains tests.
quiz.explanation: The active Package.swift and source establish ReactiveKit. The architecture guide's historical wording and future preferences do not outweigh the current edges or prove completed migration.

quiz.question: Why distinguish ApolloAPI from Apollo in an inventory?
options: They are always interchangeable names.
ApolloAPI supplies generated-model contracts while the broader client product has another role.
Generated GraphQL models cannot be used without a live network.
Every test dependency ships in the App Clip.
quiz.explanation: Product selection matters. Generated modules declare ApolloAPI, and the inspected app-test target declares Apollo. A model dependency is not proof that the whole runtime/client graph is needed by every consumer.

quiz.question: Which is a defensible migration completion statement?
options: The selected adapter preserves stated behavior; listed consumers still use the old route.
A preference for async means all promises have disappeared.
A wrapper guarantees SDK cancellation without tests.
The package version proves legal approval.
quiz.explanation: Completion should name the changed seam and its verified behavior. Preferences, wrappers, and pins do not establish cancellation, graph-wide retirement, or license decisions.

exercise.brief: Build a six-row responsibility and ownership ledger, then design and test or paper-trace one synthetic adapter contract.
steps: Choose transport, generated models, state/async, UI, identity, and observability rows from the verified map.
For each, record requirement, relevant resolution route, product, active consumer edge, responsibility, and reviewer role.
Contrast ReactiveKit evidence with the legacy guide wording and identify one retained PromiseKit bridge.
Predict CatalogFixture behavior for nonempty success, empty success, and offline failure; add cancellation as an explicit unimplemented policy.
Write a migration boundary and list evidence still needed for device, privacy, license, or human ownership.
acceptance: Every named active library has a manifest/product edge, with source imports recorded where inspected.
The ledger does not confuse package names, modules, latest versions, or test-only inclusion.
ReactiveKit and incomplete PromiseKit migration are described accurately.
Empty success and offline failure stay distinct, and async is not described as automatic background execution.
Ownership is recorded as confirmed evidence or a proposed reviewer role; no names or approvals are invented.
exercise.solution:
A worked ledger maps Alamofire to the adapter target in ZDNetworking, ApolloAPI to generated schema modules, PromiseKit and ReactiveKit to retained asynchronous contracts, SnapKit to Mezzanine/UIKit consumers, Auth0 to the authentication feature declaration, and OpenTelemetry/Sentry to ZDCore tracing and error-related targets. Each row includes its checkout pin and selected graph route. The complete unit inventory is wider than these six examples.

The CatalogFixture returns its entries for nonempty success, returns an empty successful array unchanged, and throws CatalogFailure.offline for failure. Its Result.get call preserves that distinction. It has no cancellation handler, live transport, resource lookup, or account policy. A test can check these three cases with local fixtures; passing them still leaves those missing requirements pending.

The migration statement can say that a chosen consumer would adopt a vendor-independent CatalogServing seam after behavior and lifecycle checks. It cannot say the client has migrated, because this lab changes no client source. Record the ZDRxCore naming mismatch and retained PromiseKit bridge as audit findings. Review roles are proposed until actual maintainers are confirmed. Device media, SDK data flow, selected-version licensing, and production startup measurements remain specialist or integration work.

lessons.title: Code generation, module resources, localization, and privacy manifests
lessons.summary: Trace generated output to its inputs and prove resource lookup and packaging across source packages, apps, and extensions.
objectives: Explain code-generation inputs, pinned generators, deterministic output, and source membership.
Use Bundle.module through an owning module and distinguish processing from copying resources.
Diagnose missing assets, localized strings, fonts, and duplicate bundle assumptions.
Review privacy manifests as artifact and behavior evidence without treating declaration as permission or compliance proof.

sections.title: Code can compile while the product is incomplete
sections.html:
An Android engineer expects generated R symbols, merged resources, manifest entries, and KSP or annotation-processor output to participate in a build. iOS has related concerns, but their ownership differs. A Swift module can compile while a font is absent, a JSON fixture is copied into the wrong bundle, a generated operation belongs to an obsolete schema, or an extension omits a privacy manifest. Treat code, generation inputs, and resources as parts of the same product contract.

Start each investigation with the owner. Is this resource in the app, an extension, a source-package target, or a vendor framework? Which manifest declares it? Which code chooses its bundle? Which generation step produces any accessor? A directory named Resources has meaning through the build declaration, not through its spelling alone. Likewise, a Swift file marked generated still needs active target membership and compatible dependencies.

The checkout has useful contrasting examples: the main app explicitly includes resource globs and a privacy manifest, ZDAssets declares processed package resources, the app enables assets/strings/fonts synthesizers, and the generated GraphQL packages specify source paths and ApolloAPI dependencies. These observations support different ownership paths. They do not prove the packaged app contains every file or that an old duplicate directory participates in the build. The following sections explain how to turn those declarations into a testable artifact trace.

sections.title: Pin and inspect the generator, not only the runtime
sections.html:
The active GraphQL generation script first checks that apollo-ios-cli exists and matches the version file. That file records 1.25.4, matching the inspected generated packages' exact Apollo requirement. The script then downloads both schemas, runs the schema modifier for each namespace, and generates output. This is a pipeline with distinct failure categories: tool selection, network/schema acquisition, schema transformation, operation validation, output generation, and compilation.

GqlPhi and GqlNonPhi configurations specify operation and schema search paths, schema namespaces, and output directories. Operations are emitted into their schema modules, test mocks are disabled, and pruning is enabled. The Phi configuration additionally reduces generated schema types. Pruning makes a regeneration a material write: it may remove stale generated files. Reading these settings does not authorize running the script on the client. The lab uses synthetic local inputs and leaves live schema fetches and client source unchanged.

Review a generated diff from its inputs. Was an operation changed, a schema updated, a modifier altered, or a generator version changed? A hand-edited generated model can disappear on the next run and can hide mismatch between schema and operation. Preserve intentional handwritten scalar or support code according to the generator's actual ownership rules. Record generator version, schema/input hash, configuration, and resulting diff. With the same pinned inputs, a second generation should produce no unexplained output changes; that is a reproducibility acceptance criterion, not an observation claimed in this audit.

sections.title: Several kinds of generated code need different diagnostics
sections.html:
A Swift macro transforms syntax during compilation; it is not the same operation as downloading a GraphQL schema or synthesizing an asset accessor. The vendored TestableMacro package separates a macro implementation target from the library exposing it. Its implementation consumes SwiftSyntaxMacros and SwiftCompilerPlugin, and the sibling Tuist project wires a macro dependency explicitly. This distinction matters because host compiler plugins and iOS runtime targets have different build destinations.

The active Tuist dependency manifest includes a specialized OpenTelemetryApi compiler-plugin path setting, with a comment explaining a toolchain integration issue. That is a checked-in workaround to investigate when the appropriate diagnostics appear, not a universal flag to add to every module. A missing macro implementation, invalid generated Swift, and a runtime missing resource are different failures. Inspect the earliest meaningful diagnostic and the owning generator before clearing caches.

The app enables asset, string, and font resource synthesizers and deliberately omits plist synthesis, with a documented earlier generator problem. ZDAssets sets an empty synthesizer list. Neither declaration alone settles whether a compatible Bundle.module accessor is available on a particular generated route. Verify the generated support code and compilation for that route. Do not commit a second manually created accessor merely to silence a missing symbol without understanding the generator. Session 048 will place host-tool checks and iOS integration checks into different matrix rows.

sections.title: Load from the module that owns the resource
sections.html:
Bundle.main identifies the main bundle of the running process. A package library's resources are not necessarily there, particularly under tests or a different app host. SwiftPM supplies Bundle.module for a resource-bearing target. Its generated accessor belongs to that module rather than becoming a universal lookup on every imported package. The active ZDAssets source exposes a public Bundle.assets convenience value backed by Bundle.module, giving clients a stable way to select the owner's bundle.

This synthetic manifest and library loader form a host-compatible resource package once you create the named source and test directories. Put bootstrap.json under Sources/CourseResources/Resources with title Course sandbox and schemaVersion 1. They require Foundation and the package build route; the loader is not a standalone script with a magically available module bundle.

// swift-tools-version: 5.9
import PackageDescription
let package = Package(
    name: "CourseResources",
    targets: [
        .target(
            name: "CourseResources",
            resources: [.process("Resources")]
        ),
        .testTarget(
            name: "CourseResourcesTests",
            dependencies: ["CourseResources"]
        )
    ]
)

The target owns the resource declaration and SwiftPM creates its bundle support during the build. Process asks the build system to handle supported resource transformations; copy preserves the specified resource content or directory structure. Choose according to lookup and packaging needs, rather than assuming they are interchangeable. In particular, localized resources and asset catalogs require understanding their processing rules. A static code product can still need a separate resource bundle. Always verify file presence and actual lookup instead of deducing resource behavior from the linkage choice.

sections.title: Make a missing file distinct from malformed data
sections.html:
import Foundation

enum ResourceFailure: Error, Equatable { case missing }
struct CourseBootstrap: Decodable, Equatable {
    let title: String
    let schemaVersion: Int
}

func loadBootstrap(
    named name: String = "bootstrap",
    in bundle: Bundle = .module
) throws -> CourseBootstrap {
    guard let url = bundle.url(forResource: name, withExtension: "json") else {
        throw ResourceFailure.missing
    }
    let data = try Data(contentsOf: url)
    return try JSONDecoder().decode(CourseBootstrap.self, from: data)
}

The import supplies Bundle, Data, and JSONDecoder. ResourceFailure is a separate missing-file error; a corrupt JSON document still produces the decoder's own error. Decodable requests synthesized decoding for the stored fields, while Equatable supports fixture comparison. The function's external labels are named and in; name and bundle are local parameter names. Default arguments select the known file and the module bundle, but a test can deliberately request a different name.

The guard unwraps the optional URL and exits by throwing when it is absent. Data's initializer can fail for I/O reasons, so try preserves that failure too. The final decode uses CourseBootstrap.self to pass the type as a value to the generic decoder. It does not validate that the schema version is supported by the product; that is a separate rule added in the later lab. This separation makes missing-resource, decoding, and business-contract errors observable.

Synchronous reading is acceptable for this tiny isolated fixture exercise. It is not advice to read large files or decode extensive documents on the UI thread at startup. A production implementation must budget I/O and decoding and choose an appropriate execution boundary. The Android analogy is a typed resource loader supplied with the correct Context or class loader, but Bundle.module's generated module ownership and target-specific packaging are different. Successful decoding on the host does not validate an app archive or extension bundle.

sections.title: Keep lookup identity, translation, and target inclusion aligned
sections.html:
Images, fonts, strings, nibs, and JSON can follow different build processing paths. An asset catalog produces compiled assets rather than a promise that every original file is copied unchanged. Registering a bundled font and finding its file are separate actions. A localized string lookup needs the intended table and owning bundle, and a package containing localized resources needs the appropriate default-localization declaration. A string key is not itself the translated text.

The main app declares an en.lproj folder reference among its resources, while package targets have their own processed Resources directories. Do not move a localized file between those owners while leaving the lookup unchanged. A host test may select a different Bundle.main than the installed app, and an extension is another process with another main bundle. These are common reasons a default language appears to work while a package test or alternate language fails.

Plan observable cases: the owner can find a known resource, a missing lookup fails predictably, a deliberately malformed fixture reports decoding failure, a translated key resolves under a selected locale, and missing translations follow the documented fallback. Include plural forms, substitutions, and long text in UI practice rather than assuming one English snapshot settles localization. Session 022 covers accessibility and localization behavior; this lesson adds build and bundle ownership. API-specific string-catalog adoption and translation workflows require their actual toolchain and target settings, so no repository-wide migration is implied.

sections.title: A privacy manifest declares use; it does not grant permission
sections.html:
PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy is a property-list resource describing relevant data use and required-reason API usage. It is not an entitlement, a runtime permission prompt, or the App Store privacy answers themselves. A valid declaration must reflect the actual implementation and the current permitted reason. The active app manifest includes the file in its resource list, and the inspected file declares file-timestamp and UserDefaults categories with reason entries. This establishes declarations, not a compliance verdict.

Privacy review follows the shipped code and every relevant SDK, including static dependencies whose manifests must survive packaging. An SDK update may change data collection or required-reason API use without changing your feature screen. Check the vendor artifact, aggregate privacy reporting where appropriate, the app's own declarations, and the final archive. A manifest in the repository that is absent from the packaged product is a different failure from an inaccurate reason in a packaged manifest.

Apple's current privacy-manifest and required-reason references were consulted for this lesson. Their availability does not mean the checkout pins automatically meet all current distribution requirements. Recheck policy and the selected SDK artifact before operational submission, and involve privacy specialists for actual data-flow interpretation. Do not copy a reason code from another product as a way to silence a warning. The same discipline applies to licensing notices: a resource's presence is packaging evidence, while its meaning and sufficiency require a separate review.

sections.title: Prove the chain at the appropriate boundary
sections.html:
A useful resource ledger connects input, generator if any, target membership, owning bundle, lookup code, and observation. The synthetic JSON needs only a package resource declaration and a loader. GraphQL models additionally need a schema, operations, modifier, generator pin, output path, and ApolloAPI compatibility. A macro needs its host implementation and compiler wiring. A privacy manifest needs correct content and final packaging. Putting all of these into a generic generated-files bucket hides the next useful diagnostic.

For a local package resource edit, begin with the smallest behavioral test: known fixture decoding, missing-name failure, and malformed-data behavior if a separate corrupt fixture is created. Then test integration only when the affected consumers require it. For a shared asset change that reaches the app and App Clip, add both packaging/lookup paths and representative UI checks. For a privacy SDK update, archive and inspect the privacy resources; a host model test cannot supply that evidence.

Record pending checks honestly. The audit reads active inputs and source anchors; it does not run the live GraphQL fetch, regenerate the client's code, inspect a newly built archive, or measure resource size. The worked answer gives a test pattern the learner can execute in an isolated package. Your own results, locale choices, error messages, and environment belong in the exercise submission. Source familiarity becomes useful only when you can explain which link in the chain a failure invalidated and which links remain untested.

quiz.question: Why can Bundle.main fail to find a package resource?
options: A package resource belongs to its owning module bundle, while main names the process's main bundle.
Swift never allows JSON in packages.
All static libraries discard resources.
The resource name must equal the app bundle ID.
quiz.explanation: Bundle ownership is independent of linkage and installation identity. Bundle.module is generated for the resource-bearing target; clients use the owner's API or exposed bundle rather than assuming their own main bundle contains it.

quiz.question: What does a privacy manifest included by a resource glob prove?
options: The app has every runtime permission.
The manifest is a declared build input; packaged presence and accurate declarations still need verification.
The selected SDK version is automatically compliant.
All App Store privacy answers have been submitted.
quiz.explanation: A source declaration is only one step. Permissions, entitlement authorization, accurate data-use reasons, final packaging, and store disclosures are separate concerns.

quiz.question: Why must a generated-code review include the generator version and input diff?
options: Generated files cannot compile.
Those inputs explain and reproduce the output, while hand edits may be overwritten.
Only generated files can contain tests.
A lockfile controls downloaded schema contents automatically.
quiz.explanation: Pinned generators and schema/operation/configuration inputs make output auditable. A dependency pin does not pin a live schema fetch, and generated-file edits can disappear during pruning/regeneration.

exercise.brief: Create a synthetic CourseResources package and a resource/generation ledger; keep client code and live schema endpoints untouched.
steps: Independently create the scratch manifest, library source, and bootstrap.json fixture with title Course sandbox and schemaVersion 1.
Write a decoding test and a missing-name test before comparing the worked answer.
Trace ZDAssets resources to Bundle.assets and the app privacy manifest to its resource glob.
Record GraphQL CLI pin, schema/operation inputs, modification stage, and output module membership from the active files.
State additional lookup, localization, archive, and privacy checks required for a real consumer change.
acceptance: Known resource lookup decodes the two expected synthetic fields.
A missing resource throws ResourceFailure.missing, independently of malformed-data and I/O failures.
The learner explains named/in labels, guard unwrapping, try, and CourseBootstrap.self.
The ledger distinguishes source resource declarations from packaged-artifact observations.
No live schema fetch, credential use, generated client edit, translation migration, or privacy approval is claimed.
exercise.solution:
The synthetic file contents are {"title":"Course sandbox","schemaVersion":1}. Place them in the owning target's declared Resources directory. The loader above is the worked implementation; the tests below belong in Tests/CourseResourcesTests under the retained XCTest-compatible tools baseline.

import XCTest
@testable import CourseResources

final class ResourceContractTests: XCTestCase {
    func testKnownFixture() throws {
        let value = try loadBootstrap()
        XCTAssertEqual(value.title, "Course sandbox")
        XCTAssertEqual(value.schemaVersion, 1)

            try loadBootstrap(named: "missing-course-resource")
        ) { error in
            XCTAssertEqual(error as? ResourceFailure, .missing)
        }

}

The successful case checks lookup and decoding, not merely the file's existence. The missing-name test chooses an absent filename in the same module bundle, avoiding an unreliable assumption about Bundle.main. The error cast is optional; equality with the expected case fails if the thrown type differs. A corrupt-fixture test should expect a decoding error rather than ResourceFailure.missing.
